counterexample: Counterexample to the classification asserted in step 0025: let sigma = (1 2 3 4 5 6 7) and tau = (1 2 3 4 5 7 6), both 7-cycles. Then sigma*tau^{-1} = (1 7 6), a 3-cycle. <sigma,tau> is transitive of prime degree 7, hence primitive, and a primitive group of degree n containing a 3-cycle contains A_n (Jordan), so <sigma,tau> contains A_7; since both generators are even, <sigma,tau> = A_7. So a subgroup of S_7 generated by two 7-cycles can be A_7, which the step's list omits; conversely S_7, which the step lists, can never arise (7-cycles are even).

The Heawood graph is the point-line incidence graph of the Fano plane with Aut = PGL(2,7) of order 336, and the index-2 subgroup preserving each side of the bipartition is PSL(2,7) = PGL(3,2). Adding a clique on the 7 point-vertices makes their degree 9 versus 3 on the other side, so every automorphism preserves each side setwise; such maps are exactly the side-preserving Heawood automorphisms, i.e. PSL(2,7). Aut(G) has order 168 = 2^3*3*7 with 8 Sylow 7-subgroups, so 48 elements of order 7; sigma of order 7 has orbits of size 1 or 7; n <= 13 < 14 forbids two 7-orbits and sigma != id forces one, so exactly one orbit A. 0025 FAILS. The conclusion (<sigma,tau> = Aut(G)) is true, but the stated classification is false in both directions: two 7-cycles are even permutations, so they can never generate S_7, and they CAN generate A_7 (see counterexample field), a case the step omits entirely. The case analysis as written is therefore not exhaustive and the step's conclusion does not follow from it. The gap is repairable without new ideas -- A_7 has order 2520 > 168 and is excluded by the very phrase 'gives too many automorphisms' used for S_7, and in fact <sigma,tau> lies inside Aut(G) = PSL(2,7), whose only subgroups containing elements of order 7 are C_7, F_21 and the whole group -- but as literally stated the justification rests on a false theorem.

A != B with |A| = |B| = 7 gives A\B and B\A nonempty; complementation preserves Aut, n, and the orbits A, B, so the WLOG is legitimate. tau fixes v (v not in B) and is transitive on B, so v is adjacent to all of B. The compressed 'applying sigma first' is valid: sigma fixes w (w not in A) and is transitive on A, so v'w is an edge for every v' in A, and then tau applied to v' in A\B (which tau fixes) gives all edges between A\B and B.

0033 OK modulo an evident typo ('A u B' should read 'A n B'). Identifying A with Z_7 so that sigma is x -> x+1, the induced edge set on A is a union of difference classes d in {1,2,3}; since A n B is a nonempty proper subset of A and x -> x+d is a 7-cycle for each such d, some pair at difference d straddles A n B and A\B, so every difference class is present and G[A] = K_7. The symmetric argument with tau gives G[B] = K_7, and together with the complete bipartite joins between A\B and B and between B\A and A, every pair in A u B is an edge.
